Analyse the examples:
In the examples, we have an arrow-like or chevron-like shape made of orange (7) pointing upwards.
Below it, there are some yellow (4) pixels.
Looking at example 1:
7s are:
r2: c4
r3: c3, c4, c5
r4: c2, c3, c5, c6 (hole at c4)
r5: c1, c7
Notice this chevron shape has an opening at the bottom.
The hole at r4, c4 is enclosed by 7s?
r2, c4 is 7
r3, c3, c4, c5 are 7
r4, c2, c3, c5, c6 are 7 (r4, c4 is 0)
Inside the chevron:
r4, c4 is 0.
r5, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6 are 0.
Wait, in example 1, 4s are at:
(7, 4)
(7, 8)
(9, 1)

In output 1:
4s are placed:
- Column 4 from row 4 all the way to bottom (row 9).
- Column 1 from row 6 to row 9.
Why column 4 and column 1?
Wait! Look at (9, 1) -> column 1!
In output 1, column 1 has 4 from row 6 down to 9.
Row 5 has 7 at column 1! So from row 6 to 9, it's blocked by the 7 above it?
Wait, at column 4:
4 was at (7, 4).
The 7 structure:
r2: c4
r3: c4
r4: c4 is 0, but above it is r3 c4 (7) and r2 c4 (7).
Wait, in output 1, at c4, 4 goes from row 4 to row 9!
Wait, why didn't (7, 8) extend upwards?
Wait! In example 1, (7, 8) is at c8. At c8, is it in the output?
In output 1:
(7, 8) is STILL 4! But it did NOT extend upwards or downwards!
Wait, why did (9, 1) extend upwards to row 6?
Because at row 5, col 1 is a 7!
So the 4 extends UPWARDS towards 7?
Wait, (9, 1) extends up until it hits (5, 1) (which is 7)?
Wait, (6, 1), (7, 1), (8, 1), (9, 1) are 4!
What about (7, 4)?
At (7, 4), going up: (6, 4), (5, 4), (4, 4) - at (3, 4) is 7!
And it extends DOWNWARDS too?!
Wait, (8, 4) and (9, 4) are ALSO 4!
Wait, why did (9, 1) NOT extend downwards? It was at the bottom (row 9)!
Wait, why did (7, 8) NOT extend?
Above (7, 8) is (5, 7), not col 8! Above col 8 there is NO 7!
Look at the 7s in the grid:
Columns containing 7:
r2: 4
r3: 3, 4, 5
r4: 2, 3, 5, 6
r5: 1, 7
So columns with 7s:
col 1 (at r5)
col 2 (at r4)
col 3 (at r3, r4)
col 4 (at r2, r3)
col 5 (at r3, r4)
col 6 (at r4)
col 7 (at r5)
Col 8 has NO 7!
Col 1 has a 7 at r5.
Col 4 has 7s at r2, r3.
Col 3 has 7s at r3, r4.
Col 9 has NO 7!

Now look at example 2:
4s in input 2:
(7, 4)
(7, 8)
(9, 3)
(11, 9)
In output 2:
Col 4: has 4 from row 4 to row 19 (the bottom)!
Col 3: has 4 from row 5 to row 19!
Wait, at col 3, 7 is at row 3 and row 4! So the 4 starts right below the 7 (at row 5) and goes all the way to the bottom!
At col 4, 7 is at row 2 and row 3! So the 4 starts right below the 7 (at row 4) and goes all the way to the bottom!
What about col 8 (7, 8)?
No 7 above col 8 -> it stays just (7, 8)!
What about col 9 (11, 9)?
No 7 above col 9 -> it stays just (11, 9)!

Wait! If there is a 4 in column C, AND column C has 7 above it:
Then column C gets filled with 4 from immediately below the lowest 7 in column C, down to the bottom of the grid!
Let's check example 1:
Col 1:
Input has 4 at (9, 1).
Lowest 7 in col 1 is at (5, 1).
Immediately below it is row 6!
From row 6 to bottom (row 9) is filled with 4!
Col 4:
Input has 4 at (7, 4).
Lowest 7 in col 4 is at (3, 4).
Immediately below it is row 4!
From row 4 to bottom (row 9) is filled with 4!
Col 8:
Input has 4 at (7, 8).
There is NO 7 in col 8.
So nothing changes, (7, 8) stays 4.

Check Example 2:
Col 4:
Lowest 7 in col 4 is at (3, 4).
Below it: rows 4..19 filled with 4.
Col 3:
Input has 4 at (9, 3).
Lowest 7 in col 3 is at (4, 3).
Below it: rows 5..19 filled with 4.
Col 8: no 7 above, stays (7, 8).
Col 9: no 7 above, stays (11, 9).

That is completely consistent and simple!
Let's double check if 4 extends only downwards from lowest 7:
Yes: for any column C with at least one 4, if there is a 7 in column C (specifically above it? Wait, all 7s are in the upper chevron, so any 7 in col C is above any 4 in col C).
Let `r_7` be the row of the lowest 7 in column C.
Then for every `r > r_7` to `H - 1`, set `grid[r][C] = 4`.
If there is no 7 in column C, leave the 4s in column C as they are.
